Hear, Compare, Translate

Partial synthesis, same or different, translating into solfège, reading familiar and unfamiliar patterns, and answering with patterns of your own: the skill learning sequence from discrimination into inference, Mullen’s order.

Six levels of the skill learning sequence. The first three are by ear only and come before reading; Read it and the series section add notation, and the last asks for patterns of your own. Use headphones or speakers, sing and chant out loud, and take a breath before you answer.

The order follows Andy Mullen’s: familiar patterns first, then unfamiliar ones. Where Edwin Gordon disagrees, the note under each section says so.

Partial synthesis: name the tonality or meter

You hear two series of familiar patterns with no tonality or meter set up first. Name the tonality (or meter) of each. This is still discrimination learning, so the page teaches: after you answer, or when you press Tell me, it explains what to audiate.

Sources. Gordon: at partial synthesis the teacher does not establish tonality or meter, sings the series on a neutral syllable, and gives the answers; to leave them out would wrongly bridge to generalization-verbal (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 113, 116; Reference Handbook, Tonal Unit 6, pp. 48–49). Both series share one keyality, so only the resting tone changes. Mullen’s objective: “aurally name tonality of a series of familiar patterns with teacher guidance” (MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De, p. 74). The meter explanation names the microbeats you audiate (DU DE or DU DA DI), as Mullen does (p. 85).

Same or different (generalization-aural/oral)

The tonality or meter is set up, then you hear two patterns, once each, and say whether they were the same. Start with familiar patterns; add unfamiliar ones when that is easy.

Sources. Gordon: the teacher establishes tonality on a neutral syllable and performs two patterns or sets; at an inference level the pattern is heard only once, and a student who can’t do it goes back to aural/oral (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 131–132). Gordon uses familiar and unfamiliar patterns here; Mullen starts with familiar ones, “Ss can identify if patterns are the same or different” right after the aural/oral objectives (MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De, pp. 66, 74). Students find same easier to hear than different (Gordon, p. 219).

Translate to solfège (generalization-verbal)

You hear the tonality or meter set up, then one pattern on a neutral syllable. Sing or chant it back in syllables, then check. It opens only when the verbal association objective for the same content is done.

Sources. Gordon warns against this at the verbal association level (“it is not appropriate at this level…”); it belongs to generalization-verbal, where students repeat the teacher’s neutral-syllable pattern “using tonal syllables or rhythm syllables instead” (Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 108, 132; Reference Handbook, Tonal Unit 9, Criteria 2–3, pp. 52–54). If students can’t, instruction goes back to verbal association; the teacher guides but does not give the answer first (p. 132). Gordon uses familiar and unfamiliar patterns; Mullen practises the skill with familiar patterns first (“students need practice with that skill using familiar patterns before they try it with unfamiliar patterns”, p. 66) and calls it translation (The Literate Musician, Rhythm Lessons 8, 9.3, 10.3; Harmony Lesson 9). This page follows Mullen and offers Gordon’s unfamiliar patterns as the next step.

Not checked by the page: your syllables. You judge them against the answer. Rhythm syllables are the Gordon/Froseth system: duple DU DE (divisions DU TA DE TA), triple DU DA DI (divisions DU TA DA TA DI TA).

Read it (symbolic association and generalization-symbolic)

A pattern appears in notation, drawn the way the pattern sets write it: no stems, no rhythm, no syllables. Read it in syllables, out loud, then hear it and check. Start with familiar patterns in a new order; move to unfamiliar ones once you can read the familiar ones yourself. The name it choices mix two tonalities or meters and set neither up first, so you name it from the page.

Sources. Reading comes after aural/oral, verbal association and partial synthesis, and students first read patterns they already audiate; tonal patterns are shown on the staff without syllables or rhythm, with DO found from the DO signature (Gordon, Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 117–123). Generalization-symbolic is reading “one unfamiliar pattern of a mix of familiar and unfamiliar” patterns without the teacher’s help and naming the tonality or meter; if students can’t, go back to symbolic association or composite synthesis (pp. 133–134). Mullen: “read unfamiliar patterns (on the basis of familiar patterns)” (MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De, p. 39), and reading familiar patterns in unfamiliar order in a new DO signature (The Literate Musician, Reading Lesson 3.1, pp. 122–123).

Read and write a series (composite synthesis)

Now several familiar patterns at once, and you name the tonality or meter while you read or write them. Read: a series appears; with a name it choice nothing is set up, so you name it from the page, then sing or chant it straight through. Write from dictation: hear the series, name it, then write it by choosing each pattern’s notation in order. Write from memory: the series shows for three seconds a pattern, then you write it.

Sources. Composite synthesis joins partial synthesis and symbolic association: students “audiate tonality or meter of one or more series of familiar tonal patterns or rhythm patterns in familiar or unfamiliar order as they read and write patterns”, and “read with contextual comprehension”; patterns are still read as tonal or rhythm patterns, never combined into melodic patterns (Gordon, Learning Sequences in Music, pp. 126–127). It comes before generalization-symbolic, and students who struggle there go back to it (pp. 129, 133). Mullen lists the “can do” objectives used here: read a series of familiar patterns in familiar or unfamiliar order; write a series from dictation; write a series from memory after seeing it; give the tonality or meter to a series in notation and from dictation (How to Teach the Language of Music, p. 36). Not the same as real writing: the page has you choose each pattern’s notation from the set rather than draw it on the staff, so it checks recognition of the notation, not handwriting.

Answer with your own pattern (creativity/improvisation)

You hear a pattern; answer it out loud with one of your own. Create asks only for something different in the same tonality or meter. Improvise adds a rule: the same function, the other function, or (in rhythm) a division. There is no single right answer: the page can play or list answers from the set that fit, and you judge your own.

Sources. Creativity sets few restrictions; improvisation adds more, such as function (Gordon, Learning Sequences in Music, p. 136; Mullen, MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De, pp. 40–41, from exploration through creativity and improvisation to composition). A tonal answer has as many patterns as the teacher’s; a rhythm answer need not (Gordon, pp. 138–139). Answering on a neutral syllable is creativity/improvisation-aural/oral, which Mullen bridges to straight after aural/oral; answering in syllables comes after verbal association (Mullen, pp. 66–67, 74). Gordon’s Reference Handbook places no restriction on a creative response beyond being tonal, sets function rules for improvisation, and asks the teacher to be lenient, because bridging to an inference level reinforces the discrimination level it came from (Tonal Unit 3, pp. 43–45).

About the patterns and sound

  • Tonal, familiar: Mullen’s familiar patterns in a familiar order (FPIFO), major and minor tonic and dominant, 15 each (The Literate Musician, pp. 57, 59). They are also on Tonal Patterns as mullen-fpifo-major and mullen-fpifo-minor, with solfège, for verbal association practice.
  • Tonal, unfamiliar: the site’s Register-style sets (322a, 322b, 322b-major), tonic and dominant only.
  • Dorian and Mixolydian: the site’s tonic/subtonic sets (323a, 324a).
  • Rhythm: the site’s duple (2/4) and triple (6/8) macro/microbeat and division sets, chanted on one pitch.
  • Tonality is set with the tonal sequence 5 6 5 4 3 2 7 1 at double speed (Gordon, Reference Handbook, p. 33; Mullen, p. 79). Meter is set with two bars of microbeats and two of macrobeats; that chant is this site’s own.
  • Every pitch in a tonal pattern has the same length and every rhythm pattern uses one pitch, as in learning sequence activities (Gordon, p. 223). Resting tones stay between D and G above middle C, in the singing range Gordon gives (Reference Handbook, p. 32).
  • The instruments stand in for the neutral syllables “bum” and “bah”.

Gordon, Edwin E. Jump Right In: The Music Curriculum. Reference Handbook for Using Learning Sequence Activities. 2001 revision, GIA Publications, 2001. Tonal sequences (p. 33) and range (p. 32); Tonal Unit 6, partial synthesis (pp. 48–49); Tonal Unit 9, generalization-verbal (pp. 52–54); rhythm patterns and sequences chanted with expressive inflection on one pitch, all durations without pitch (“A Quick Course on Rhythm” and “Techniques for Teaching Class Patterns”).

Gordon, Edwin E. Learning Sequences in Music: A Contemporary Music Learning Theory. 2012 ed., GIA Publications, 2012. Skill learning sequence: partial synthesis (pp. 111–117), the verbal association warning (p. 108), generalization-aural/oral and -verbal (pp. 131–133); same is easier to hear than different (p. 219); tonal and rhythm patterns kept apart (p. 223); rhythm patterns chanted with vocal inflection like speech (p. 101); macrobeats stressed, not accented, and approached with a decrescendo, expression found between macrobeats, anacruses given special attention, weight and flow, displaced energy in rests and long durations (pp. 187–190).; Theory Concepts pages: Keyality versus key signature (p. xiii); tonality “best refers to what is usually called a mode,” the eight tonalities (p. 149); movable-do with la-based minor and the rhythm syllables du de, du da di (p. 105); resting tone and tonic, a tonality in any keyality (p. 150); unitonal and multitonal music (pp. 152, 157); usual duple, triple and combined meter (pp. 175–176); no direct relation between measure signatures and meter, 6/8 as “duple compound” called inaccurate (p. 176); accents and microbeat divisions do not make meter (pp. 176–177); unusual meter, paired and unpaired, intact, macrobeats versus microbeats establishing meter (pp. 179–180); key signatures as do signatures, one signature for many tonalities (pp. 155–156); rhythm syllables by beat function (p. 86); time-value names lead to counting (p. 38); writing tonal patterns from a familiar do signature (p. 125); letter names and time-value names as the alphabet of music (pp. 36–37); interval names learned in context of tonality and keyality (p. 65); the raised seventh of harmonic minor as si (p. 70); mi si ti re as a harmonic minor dominant pattern (p. 100).; Course pages (glossary, enrichment): audiation defined and compared with imitation (Introduction; pp. 3, 9); notation as a window (p. 8); patterns as units of meaning (pp. 99–100); the aural/oral level and the pause (pp. 101–102); discrimination and inference learning, theory delayed (p. 106); levels of the skill learning sequence (from pp. 111, 117, 126, 129, 136, 141); stepwise and bridging movement, Table 17 (pp. 230–231).; Hearing Harmony: four stages of readiness for chord changes (p. 305); harmonic patterns I V7 I, I IV I, I II V7 I, I II7 V7 I (p. 313); I V7 I, then I IV I, then I IV V7 I and I V7 IV I in three sung parts, then harmonic minor (pp. 318–319); easy and moderately difficult harmonic patterns, the supertonic delayed (p. 320).

Mullen, Andy. MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De: Teacher’s Guide to “The Literate Musician.” The Improving Musician, 2021. Bridging and familiar patterns before unfamiliar ones at generalization (pp. 65–67); the audiation-foundation objectives (p. 74); the tonal sequence (p. 79); partial synthesis in rhythm by naming the microbeat (p. 85); rhythm patterns kept conversational, inflected with style and panache (p. 84).

Mullen, Andy. The Literate Musician: How to Hear, Speak, Think, Read & Write the Language of Music. Revised 2nd ed., The Improving Musician, 2020. FPIFO, major and minor tonic and dominant (pp. 57, 59), copied into mullen-fpifo-major / -minor in apps/patterns/pattern-set.js; FPIFO in the Dorian, Mixolydian, Phrygian, Lydian, Aeolian and Locrian tonalities (pp. 22–27), mullen-fpifo-dorian … -locrian, with the keys moved so that C is the book’s resting tone; Major and Minor Subdominant FPIFO (p. 293), mullen-subdominant-major / -minor; the stepwise sets (pp. 71–72) are the site’s major-stepwise / minor-stepwise; rhythm patterns by lesson (duple and triple macrobeat and microbeat, pp. 37, 39–40; divisions, pp. 45, 47; elongation cells, pp. 48–49), copied into the mullen-rhythm-* sets of apps/rhythms/rhythm-pattern-object.js; translation lessons (Rhythm 8, 9.3, 10.3; Harmony 9); Hearing Harmony: Harmony lessons 2–5 (major and minor tonic and dominant, pp. 53–58), 7 (comparing major and minor, p. 62), the Harmonic Loops by tonality (pp. 20–27).
